name: Rialto Bridge
label: Rialto Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Riva del Vin' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Riva del Vin nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2289364: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Rialto Bridge' (84 m across).
notes: The oldest and most famous bridge over the Grand Canal.

text.description:
The Rialto Bridge is the oldest of the four bridges across the Grand Canal, and it links the districts of San Marco and San Polo. The stone bridge you see today is a single broad arch designed by Antonio da Ponte, built between 1588 and 1591. Two covered ramps rise to a central portico, and both ramps are lined with small shops. At the time, the engineering was thought so daring that one architect predicted it would fall down. It has stood for more than four centuries. Before it, a series of earlier crossings stood here, starting with a floating pontoon bridge and followed by a wooden one that collapsed more than once.

It photographs well because the shape is so clear. From the San Polo bank on Riva del Vin you see the bridge side-on, with the whole arch, the little shops in the span and the Grand Canal below. Vaporetti and other boats pass through the frame, and on a calm morning the arch reflects in the water. That makes a good busy-but-tidy scene for a phone. Aim to include a bit of water in the foreground, and wait a moment for a boat to move into a gap rather than cutting across the bridge. If you want a different feel, Riva del Ferro gives a view from water level, and Riva del Carbon gives a three-quarter view that works well as the lights come on in the evening.
text.geographic_location: The Rialto Bridge crosses the Grand Canal in the middle of Venice, joining the San Polo bank to the San Marco bank.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so start from the San Polo side of the Grand Canal, which is the south-west bank, and walk along the canal-side street called Riva del Vin. The bridge is then just a moment's walk to the east. If you are coming from further out, take a taxi (in Venice, a water taxi) to the Rialto area and walk the last part. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the side-on view of the arch. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to include more of the canal and the boats. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the arch and the shops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Riva del Vin (San Polo (south-west) bank, facing the bridge side-on). The bridge's single arch seen from the side, with the Grand Canal, passing vaporetti and reflections in the water. The bridge is to the east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the waterline on the lower third, so that the arch fills the middle of the picture and there is a bit of water in front of it. Keep the phone level, since the long line of the bridge makes a tilt obvious. Wait for a boat to come into a gap in the scene. If the first spot is too crowded, Riva del Ferro (at water level) and Riva del Carbon (a three-quarter view) are alternatives.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the arch to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky and the lit water don't wash out. In the blue hour, use night mode and rest your elbows on something steady, since boats move and will blur in a long exposure.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise (about 6:30-7:30) or the blue hour, when the water is usually calm and the reflections are clearest. By midday Riva del Vin can be crowded.

text.access_note: The bridge and the Riva del Vin quayside are open public places, but check the official site before you go if you plan anything beyond the viewpoint, such as rooftop terraces nearby.

name: Bridge of Sighs
label: Bridge of Sighs
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ponte della Paglia' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ponte della Paglia' (way/431014237): middle (38 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/138803225: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bridge of Sighs' (12 m across).
notes: Enclosed limestone bridge between the Doge's Palace and the prison.

text.description:
The Bridge of Sighs is a small, enclosed bridge of white Istrian limestone that links the Doge's Palace with the New Prison across the Rio di Palazzo. The architect Antonio Contin designed it, and it was built soon after 1600. Inside, two separate walkways kept prisoners being taken to court apart from those already convicted. The romantic name is a 19th-century invention, given in English by Lord Byron, who translated it from the Italian.

It photographs well because it is so compact. A single arch sits under a decorated roofline, with a row of carved heads along the arch and two stone-latticed windows on each side. From the right spot, the pale bridge is framed by the palace on one side and the prison building on the other, with the canal below. Gondolas often pass underneath, which adds scale and life to the picture.

The classic view is from Ponte della Paglia, looking up the canal. Start with the default lens (1x) so the bridge sits between the two buildings, then try a zoom to pick out the windows and carving. Keep the phone steady against the parapet and wait for a gap in the crowds or a gondola to drift into the frame. A second option is a more level-ground view from the Riva degli Schiavoni waterfront promenade.
text.geographic_location: The bridge is in Venice, spanning the Rio di Palazzo between the Doge's Palace and the New Prison.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the Doge's Palace. Stand on Ponte della Paglia and look north up the Rio di Palazzo. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main postcard shot. Switch to the telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) for a tighter view of the windows and carved heads. The ultra-wide (0.5x) takes in more of the palace and canal but makes the bridge look small and the crowd look bigger.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ponte della Paglia (stand on the bridge and look north up the Rio di Palazzo). The Bridge of Sighs framed between the Doge's Palace on one side and the Prigioni Nuove on the other, with the canal below and gondolas passing underneath.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the bridge in the centre, keeping the two buildings roughly balanced on either side. Hold the phone upright for the bridge and canal, or turn it sideways for more of the palace wall. Wait for a gondola to pass beneath the arch. For a different angle, try the longer side view from Ponte della Canonica, or a level-ground view from Riva degli Schiavoni, and check the angle when you arrive.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white stone of the bridge to set focus and exposure, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or water is washing out the stone. If a gondola is passing, take a Live Photo or a quick burst so you can choose the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, around sunrise (about 6:00-8:00am), when the crowds are thinnest. Late afternoon is also suggested. Crowds build from mid-morning, so midday is the hardest time to get a clear frame.

text.access_note: Ponte della Paglia is a public bridge, free and open at all hours, though it may be reached by a few small steps; going inside the Bridge of Sighs is part of the Doge's Palace visit, so check the official site before you go.

name: Doge's Palace
label: Doge's Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ponte della Paglia' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ponte della Paglia' (way/431014237): middle (38 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/138803915: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Doge's Palace' (183 m across).
notes: Gothic palace of the Venetian rulers beside the lagoon.

text.description:
The Doge's Palace is the great Venetian Gothic building beside St Mark's Basilica. It was once the home of the Doge and also held government offices and a jail. A first palace was built in 810, the Gothic rebuilding began around 1340, and it has been a museum since 1923. It photographs well for two reasons: the long Gothic facade is easy to recognise, and the waterside corner sits beside a canal and the enclosed Bridge of Sighs, which has linked the palace to the prison since the 16th century.

From this bridge, beside the palace's south-east corner, you see the waterside corner and facade, with the Bridge of Sighs across the Rio di Palazzo. It is the standard outside angle on that bridge, and looking from the street costs nothing. If you want the palace in its full width, Piazza San Marco is a good second choice. There the long facade is framed by open paving, with the Basilica beside it.

Expect other people on the bridge, so be patient and shoot between groups. The inside views, such as the Giants' Staircase, need a palace ticket, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In Venice, on the waterfront beside St Mark's Basilica.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed for this spot, so start near St Mark's Basilica and walk to the waterfront side to find Ponte della Paglia. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the corner of the palace and the Bridge of Sighs together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the bridge is crowded and you cannot step back. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter picture of the Bridge of Sighs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ponte della Paglia (bridge beside the palace's southeast corner, over the Rio di Palazzo). The palace's waterside corner and facade, with the enclosed Bridge of Sighs linking to the prison building across the canal. For the full width of the facade, you can also walk into Piazza San Marco.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the palace corner with one of the vertical lines, so the building does not lean. Leave the Bridge of Sighs in the upper part of the frame and some water at the bottom. For a different view, take a wide shot of the whole facade from Piazza San Marco.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few frames in a row, because people keep moving across the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, though the bridge is never empty.

text.access_note: The outside views from Ponte della Paglia and Piazza San Marco are free from the street, but the palace itself is a ticketed museum, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Ponte della Paglia is the standard outside angle on the Bridge of Sighs and viewing it from the street is free.
Early-morning crowds are lighter but not absent.
Ponte della Paglia can be crowded, with people moving across it.
A palace ticket is needed for the interior views such as the Giants' Staircase.
Slightly lowering the exposure helps when the sky is bright, and gridlines help keep verticals straight.

name: Piazza San Marco
label: Piazza San Marco
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Campanile di San Marco' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Campanile di San Marco' (way/252637693): middle (23 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/172349507: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Mark's Square' (280 m across).

text.description: Piazza San Marco is the main square of Venice and, together with the little Piazzetta running down to the water, the city's social, religious and political centre. It photographs well because everything is gathered in one frame: the basilica with its arches, marble and four horses at the eastern end, long arcades down both sides, and the Campanile standing free in the open space. The Campanile dates from 1156-73. It collapsed on 14 July 1902 and was rebuilt in 1912 'as it was, where it was'. The Clocktower, finished in 1499, marks the start of the Merceria shopping route towards the Rialto. The best way to see the whole layout is from the top of the Campanile, reached by lift. Guides rate it as one of the best views down onto the square, with the Doge's Palace, the basilica roofs, the lagoon and red rooftops beyond. It is ticketed, so check the official site before you go. For a ground-level frame, the basilica façade with the Campanile beside it is the classic shot, but some guides say stalls and crowds spoil it after about 8 AM. Punta della Dogana, across the water, is a good alternative for the square, the Doge's Palace and the Campanile together.
text.geographic_location: At the heart of Venice, with St Mark's Basilica at its eastern end and the Piazzetta leading south to the lagoon between the Doge's Palace and the Biblioteca Marciana.
text.directions_text: Piazza San Marco is the centre of Venice. Plan to arrive on foot, for example by following the Merceria from the Rialto and passing through the archway under the Clocktower. The Campanile top is the recommended high viewpoint. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole square and the lagoon. Then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as the Doge's Palace, the basilica roofs or boats on the water. The default lens (1x) suits a balanced view of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Campanile di San Marco (top of the bell tower, reached by lift). A sweeping view down onto the square, the Doge's Palace and the basilica roofs, with the lagoon and red rooftops beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the horizon and the edges of the square level. Include a strip of the lagoon at the top and the arcades below to give a sense of scale. For a second picture, zoom in on the basilica roofs or the Doge's Palace. If you would rather shoot from ground level, Punta della Dogana across the water shows the square, the Doge's Palace and the Campanile together.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the square to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Try panorama mode for a sweep across the whole view, moving slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides say the ground-level view is clearest early, before about 8 AM, before stalls and crowds build up. For the tower view, check the official site for current times before you go.

text.access_note: The square is open public space, but the Campanile lift is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: St Mark's Basilica
label: St Mark's Basilica
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza San Marco' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza San Marco' (way/172349507): middle (279 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/138800932: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St Mark's Basilica' (117 m across).
notes: The golden Byzantine cathedral on Piazza San Marco.

text.description:
St Mark's Basilica is the cathedral church of Venice and holds the relics of Saint Mark, the city's patron saint. It stands at the eastern end of St Mark's Square and is attached to the Doge's Palace. Before 1797 it was the Doge's own chapel. The present building was probably begun in 1063. Its design was modelled on a church in Constantinople, and over the centuries it was dressed in marble and carvings, many of them brought back from that city. Four ancient bronze horses were set above the entrance.

It photographs well because the west front is so rich. Five portals, gold mosaics and the horses all sit in one frame, and from the middle of the square you can also fit in the Campanile and the Doge's Palace. The mosaics inside span about eight hundred years of artistic styles, but interior photography is not allowed, so make the square your main picture.

A wide shot of the whole front works best from the open paving. Come back with a closer shot of the portals and the mosaics above them. If you want an alternative, the Ala Napoleonica frames a view through its arch across the square to the basilica. The Loggia dei Cavalli gives close views of the facade at eye level, but access may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The basilica stands at the eastern end of St Mark's Square (Piazza San Marco) in Venice, attached to the Doge's Palace and with the Campanile close by.
text.directions_text: Make for Piazza San Marco, the big open square in front of the basilica. The last part of the journey to the square is on foot. Once you are on the open paving in the middle of the square, between the Campanile and the basilica, you are. The basilica is about 95 m to the east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the basilica, the Campanile and the arcades into one shot. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view of the west front alone. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the mosaics, the portals and the bronze horses.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza San Marco (open paving in the middle of the square, between the Campanile and the basilica). The west front of the basilica with its five portals, gold mosaics, and bronze horses, with the Doge's Palace and the Campanile in the same frame. Face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the basilica centred so the verticals stay straight. Turn the phone sideways for the whole front, then upright if you want to include the Campanile. Telephoto shots of the mosaics need no tripod, so brace your elbows against your body. For a different angle, the Ala Napoleonica gives a view through its arch across the empty square to the basilica.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright gold mosaics to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the gold keeps its detail. Try panorama mode for the full width of the square, and hold the phone steady and upright as you sweep.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before about 8:00 to 9:00, when the square is emptier and the light is softer.

text.access_note: The square is open public space, but the basilica is a working place of worship where interior photography is prohibited, and the terrace may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Venice's historic centre is largely pedestrian, so the last part of the journey to the square is on foot.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail in the bright gold mosaics.
Modest dress is usually expected at a place of worship, so entry rules and dress code should be checked on the official site.
A phone held steadily and kept upright gives a better panorama sweep.

name: Grand Canal
label: Grand Canal
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ponte dell'Accademia' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ponte dell'Accademia' (way/556239027): middle (96 m across); moved 30 m off water.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: The main waterway lined with palaces.

text.description:
The Grand Canal is the main water street of Venice. It is 3.8 kilometres long and between 30 and 90 metres wide, and it winds through the city in a big reverse S from the railway station to the basin at San Marco. More than 170 buildings line its banks, most of them from the 13th to the 18th century, built by noble families who wanted their palazzi to show off their wealth. Many palaces rise straight out of the water with no pavement, so the full sweep of façades is best seen from the canal itself.

For a phone photo, the classic place is the Ponte dell'Accademia, one of only four bridges over the canal. Looking east from the middle of the bridge, the canal opens out in front of you. The domed church of Santa Maria della Salute sits as the natural focal point, and palazzi line both banks. The long view gives your picture depth, and boats passing on the water add scale and movement. Lean on the side of the bridge to keep your phone steady, and keep the dome slightly off-centre so the canal leads the eye towards it.

If you have time for a second picture, Riva del Vin shows the Rialto Bridge side-on, with reflections in the water. Fondamenta della Salute gives a view across the water towards the San Marco bell tower.
text.geographic_location: The Grand Canal runs through the central districts (sestieri) of Venice, from the Santa Lucia railway station to the basin at San Marco. The Ponte dell'Accademia is one of its bridges, with the Salute church downstream to the east.
text.directions_text: From the Santa Lucia railway station, use your phone map to walk to the Ponte dell'Accademia, or take a water bus along the canal and get off nearby. Streets in Venice twist a lot, so keep your phone map open for the last stretch and look for the Ponte dell'Accademia on the map. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full canal view. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the Salute dome closer. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the bridge's railing and a lot of sky in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ponte dell'Accademia (facing east, toward the Basilica di Santa Maria della Salute). A sweeping view down the Grand Canal with the domed Salute church as the focal point and palazzi lining both banks. From the bridge, face east down the canal towards the Salute.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the canal along the centre line so the banks lead towards the dome. Keep a little water in the foreground and let a passing boat enter one third of the frame. For a different angle, try Riva del Vin for the Rialto Bridge side-on, or Fondamenta della Salute for gondolas with the San Marco bell tower across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the dome to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour at sunset. At blue hour, use night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to stay steady. Wait for boats to pass before pressing the shutter, or use a Live Photo to pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset and blue hour. The bridge is very busy in high season, so an early or late visit gives you more room to take photos.

text.access_note: The Ponte dell'Accademia is a public bridge, free to use and open at all hours; for boat rides on the canal, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Water buses (vaporetti) run along the Grand Canal.
When facing east at sunset, the sun is behind you and lights the palazzi.
The bridge is crowded in high season, so early or late visits are quieter.

name: La Fenice
label: La Fenice
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rio della Veste' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Rio Veste' (pois); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/251501878: the OpenStreetMap point 'Teatro La Fenice'.

text.description:
La Fenice, which means "The Phoenix", is one of Venice's best-known opera houses. The name goes back to the company that built it, which had lost its earlier theatre and wanted to rise again. The new house opened in May 1792 to a design by Giannantonio Selva. It has since burned down twice, in 1836 and again in 1996, and each time it was rebuilt. Many famous operas by Rossini, Bellini, Donizetti and Verdi were first performed here.

For photographs there are two good approaches. The classic one is the neoclassical front on Campo San Fantin. Look for the Phoenix emblem above the main door and the niche statues of Dance and Music. The square is small and easy to walk past, so it is worth checking the map. Here neighbouring buildings and small bridges frame the water, and you get a calm Venetian scene with the theatre's story close by. Photo guides say this canal is nearly empty early in the morning.

Take a few frames of each view. The front gives you the architecture and the details. The back gives you atmosphere, and reflections are possible if the water is calm. The two views are close together.
text.geographic_location: La Fenice stands in the San Marco district of Venice, between Campo San Fantin and a quiet canal.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or vaporetto stop is listed for this spot. Start from the San Marco area and head for the theatre; the final approach is on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the canal scene. It keeps the buildings and bridges looking natural. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) on Campo San Fantin if you cannot step back far enough to fit the whole facade in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rio della Veste (behind the theatre, San Marco side). A small canal scene behind the theatre, with neighbouring buildings and bridges framing the water. The theatre is to the north-west. Check the map for the exact spot along the canal.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water in the lower third. Let the buildings and bridges make a frame on either side. For the front of the theatre, an alternative is Campo San Fantin. There you can photograph the facade with the Phoenix emblem above the door and the statues in their niches. Keep your phone level so the vertical lines stay straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or a wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out. In a narrow canal, hold the phone steady and wait for the water to settle before you shoot, or use a Live Photo and pick the sharpest frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when guides say the canal is nearly empty.

text.access_note: The canal-side street and the square in front are public, but the theatre interior is only open on tours and for performances, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The theatre interior can be photographed on daytime tours but not during performances (the tour needs a ticket, so check the official site).
Holding the phone steady and waiting for the water to settle gives a sharper canal image, and reflections are possible only if the water is calm.
No nearby station or stop is listed for this spot, so the final approach is simply on foot.

name: Palazzo Contarini del Bovolo
label: Scala del Bovolo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Corte Contarina del Bovolo' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Corte Contarini del Bovolo' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2766982: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palazzo Contarini del Bovolo' (59 m across).
notes: Palace known for its spiral outdoor staircase.

text.description:
The Palazzo Contarini del Bovolo is a small 15th-century palace, and it is known for the spiral staircase on its outside wall. The staircase is a tower of stacked arches, and its name, Scala del Bovolo, means 'of the snail'. It was added in 1499 and is believed to be the work of Giorgio Spavento. The palace was built for the Contarini family and designed by Giovanni Candi. Orson Welles used it as Brabantio's house in his 1952 film of Othello, and the staircase features prominently.

It photographs well because the arches repeat in a tight rhythm, with warm stone against a strip of sky. The setting is a small courtyard off a quiet lane, so the tower fills the frame and nothing much gets in the way. Guides describe this as the standard photo, and shots taken from below often work best.

The courtyard is tight, so use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the whole tower in. Keep your phone upright and level so the tower does not lean. If the courtyard is busy, wait a moment for a gap. The staircase has been open to visitors since February 2016 after restoration, but check the official site before you go. A second angle is from Ponte de la Verona, looking across the canal toward the tower. Confirm that view on the spot before relying on it.
text.geographic_location: The palazzo sits in a small, quiet calle near Campo Manin in central Venice. It is roughly half-way between Campo San Bartolo, at the foot of the Rialto, and Campo Santo Stefano.
text.directions_text: Head for Campo Manin, then take the narrow lane from its south side to the courtyard (Corte Contarina del Bovolo). Campo San Bartolo (by the Rialto) and Campo Santo Stefano are each a walk away on either side. The lane is narrow. Look for it on the south side of Campo Manin. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole tower in. Then try the default lens (1x) for a tighter shot of a few arches. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Corte Contarina del Bovolo (corner of the courtyard furthest from the tower). The spiral staircase rising above you, with its stacked arches framing sky and stone. The tower is to the north-west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Point the phone upward and turn on gridlines. Line up a vertical grid line with the tower so it stands straight. Include a little sky above the top arches for contrast. For a different view, Ponte de la Verona gives a look across the canal toward the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white. If the walls are in deep shade, raise the exposure slightly instead. Hold the phone still against your body for sharper shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check on the day for a quiet time in the lane. Choose a time when some light reaches the upper arches, so they stand out against the shaded walls.

text.access_note: The courtyard and staircase are in a small lane, and the staircase is a visitable attraction, so check the official site before you go for access details.

name: Caffè Florian
label: Caffè Florian
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza San Marco' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza San Marco' (way/172349507): middle (279 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/12453807859: the OpenStreetMap point 'Caffè Florian'.
notes: Historic café under the arcades of Piazza San Marco.

text.description: Caffè Florian sits in the Procuratie Nuove arcade on Piazza San Marco, and guides describe the square's arcades and café terraces as prime photo ground. The row of arches and the tables set out beneath them make up the scene. It opened on 29 December 1720 as "Alla Venezia Trionfante" and soon took the name of its first owner, Floriano Francesconi. It is the oldest coffee house in continuous operation in Italy. Over the years the rooms were redecorated and added to, so inside there are painted halls, a Hall of Mirrors and an art nouveau room with hand-painted mirrors. From the square you photograph the outside: the arcaded front, the tables and the people sitting at them. The orchestra plays on the terrace from April to October, which adds atmosphere but can also crowd the square. Take a few steps back so the arches sit evenly in the frame, and include a little of the paving to give a sense of the space. If you want the interior, the gilded mirrors and painted walls are the draw, but you would need to be a customer inside, and photography rules can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Caffè Florian is in the San Marco district of Venice, under the Procuratie Nuove arcade on the edge of Piazza San Marco, facing the square with St Mark's Basilica at its far end.
text.directions_text: Head for Piazza San Marco and walk the last stretch. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the café front, then switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the arcade in the same shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza San Marco (open paving in front of the Procuratie Nuove arcade, facing the café's facade). The café's arcaded facade and its tables under the arches, with the St Mark's Basilica filling the square's far end. The basilica is to the east, behind you, so it will not appear in this view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the arches with the vertical lines so the facade does not lean. Keep the tables and the arcade as your main subject. If you want an alternative, go inside the café, where the gilded mirrors and painted rooms make good close shots near the windows and entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the arcade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the bright sky does not wash out the stonework. If people walk through the frame, take a Live Photo or a short burst and pick the cleanest shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning gives cleaner views before the crowds arrive; early evening gives warmer light and a livelier square.

text.access_note: The square is open to the public, but the café is a private business and its interior is for customers, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) fits more of the arcade into the frame than the default lens (1x).
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep bright sky from washing out the stonework.
Photography rules inside the café may change, so visitors should check them first.
Keeping the gridlines on helps stop the arches leaning in the frame.

name: Ponte dell'Accademia
label: Accademia Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Campo della Carità' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Campo de la Carità' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/556239027: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Academia Bridge' (96 m across).
notes: Wooden bridge with a classic Grand Canal view toward the Salute.

text.description: The Ponte dell'Accademia is one of only four bridges that cross the Grand Canal in Venice, and the present bridge is built of timber. It links Dorsoduro with San Marco and is named after the art academy that once shared the nearby Scuola della Carità with the Gallerie dell'Accademia. The first steel bridge opened in 1854. The present wooden one, designed by Eugenio Miozzi, opened in 1933, and many people at the time had hoped for stone. Most visitors photograph the view from the bridge. This spot is about photographing the bridge itself, which is easier to do from the Dorsoduro bank at its foot. From there you look up at the timber arch and its supports, with the dome of Santa Maria della Salute behind. The wood, water and dome make an easy layered picture with clear foreground, middle and background. A second option is the Accademia vaporetto stop, where you can shoot the underside of the bridge and its wooden pilings with boats passing in front. That view is from the water side, so it may be awkward to use on foot. Be patient, as the bridge can be busy.
text.geographic_location: In the Dorsoduro district, where the wooden bridge crosses the Grand Canal near its southern end, beside the Gallerie dell'Accademia. The far end of the bridge meets the San Marco district.
text.directions_text: Head for the Dorsoduro district and the Gallerie dell'Accademia; the bridge starts right beside it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the bridge with the Salute dome behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole timber structure and some of the water in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x) to pick out the dome, or to isolate the wooden detail of the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Campo della Carità (Dorsoduro end, at the foot of the bridge, on the bank). A low-angle view of the bridge's wooden structure with the Salute dome visible behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Crouch a little and hold the phone low so the timber arch rises above you and the dome sits just behind it. Turn on the gridlines and line the bridge up with one of the thirds rather than centring it. If you also want the underside of the bridge with its pilings and passing boats, the Accademia vaporetto stop is a second option.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the dome or the sky to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky does not wash out against the dark wood. Try a Live Photo to catch boats passing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the light is soft rather than harsh, so the timber keeps its detail and the sky does not wash out.

text.access_note: The bridge and the bank at its foot are open public space, but ground-level walkways beside the water can close during high water in late autumn and winter, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Salute dome appears behind the bridge from the foot of the bridge on the Campo della Carità side (from the researched viewpoint notes).
The bridge can be busy.
The Accademia vaporetto stop gives a view of the underside of the bridge but may be hard to use on foot.
Soft light is better for the timber and sky than harsh light (general photography advice).
The bridge and the bank are open public space with no ticket needed.
Walkways beside the water can close during high water (acqua alta) in late autumn and winter.

name: St Mark's Campanile
label: St Mark's Campanile
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza San Marco' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza San Marco' (way/172349507): middle (279 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/7578687313: the OpenStreetMap point 'Saint Mark's Campanile'.
notes: The tall brick bell tower with views over Venice.

text.description:
St Mark's Campanile is the bell tower of St Mark's Basilica, and at 98.6 metres it is the tallest structure in Venice. It began life in the early tenth century as a watchtower and a landmark for ships coming into the harbour. The tower you see today is a reconstruction finished in 1912, after the earlier one collapsed in 1902. It is a plain square brick shaft, topped by a belfry and a pointed spire with a golden weather vane in the shape of the archangel Gabriel. It stands on its own in the square, close to the front of the basilica.

It photographs well because of that simple, upright shape. Against the basilica's facade and domes it gives you a frame with both height and detail. The square is open, so you can try several angles, and a few steps to the side changes how the tower sits against the basilica. The tower is very tall for a phone, so stand back, keep the phone level and let the sky fill the top of the picture. For a second view, the Riva degli Schiavoni on the waterfront can show the Campanile above moored gondolas. Check the exact spot on the day. Early morning is the calmest time, with softer light and fewer people walking through your frame.
text.geographic_location: In St Mark's Square (Piazza San Marco), close to the basilica and near the mouth of the Grand Canal.
text.directions_text: Head on foot for the St Mark's Square area near the mouth of the Grand Canal. Once in the square, the tower is hard to miss. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the tower beside the basilica. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole height in one frame, or use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the belfry and the golden weather vane.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza San Marco. The Campanile rising beside the basilica, with the basilica's facade and domes in the same frame. From here the Campanile rises beside the basilica, with the basilica's facade and domes in the same frame, and the tower lies to the south-east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line, keeping the phone level so the sides don't lean in. Leave the basilica's facade and domes on one side of the frame and the tower on the other. If you want a different view, the Riva degli Schiavoni shows gondolas in the foreground with the Campanile standing above the waterfront behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick of the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the gold at the top keeps its detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds, when the light is softer and the square is thinner of people.

text.access_note: The square is open public space, but climbing the tower is a paid, ticketed visit and it can close in high winds or cold weather, so check the official site before you go.

name: Santa Maria della Salute
label: Santa Maria Salute
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ponte dell'Accademia' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ponte dell'Accademia' (way/556239027): middle (96 m across); moved 30 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/138801509: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Santa Maria della Salute' (86 m across).
notes: Baroque domed church at the mouth of the Grand Canal.

text.description: Santa Maria della Salute is the big white domed church at the mouth of the Grand Canal, on the tip of Dorsoduro where the canal meets the open water in front of St Mark's. It photographs well because it sits on its own at the end of the canal. Its octagonal body, two domes and statue-topped front make a strong shape, and the water around it gives you space and reflections. The Republic of Venice vowed to build it after the plague of 1630, which killed nearly a third of the city's people. Baldassare Longhena designed it, work began in 1631 and it was finished in 1681. The church stands on a platform of about a million wooden piles, and its dome has been a favourite with painters from Canaletto to Turner. The classic view is from the Ponte dell'Accademia, looking down the canal with the dome framed at the far end. It is a popular spot, so allow time to find a gap at the railing. If the bridge is too busy, Punta della Dogana shows the church beside the old customs house, and Calle del Traghetto Vecchio gives a front-on view across the water with gondolas in the foreground. Each year on 21 November the city holds the Festa della Madonna della Salute, when a temporary pontoon bridge crosses the Grand Canal to the church. If you are in Venice then, it is worth a look.
text.geographic_location: In the Dorsoduro district, on the Punta della Dogana at the entrance to the Grand Canal, between the Grand Canal and the Giudecca Canal and facing St Mark's across the water.
text.directions_text: The church is about 450 m to the east of the bridge in a straight line, so check a map for the walking route if you want to stand at the church itself. During the November festival a pontoon bridge crosses the Grand Canal to the church. Check the current crossing arrangements on the day, and check locally for boat options. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the canal, the palaces and the dome together. Switch to telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the domes. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole bridge scene, as it makes the church look small and distant.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ponte dell'Accademia (apex of the bridge, western railing facing northeast). The Salute dome framed at the end of the Grand Canal, with the canal sweeping toward the lagoon below. The basilica is to the east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the dome near one of the upper grid intersections, with the canal running in from the lower corner as a leading line. Keep the phone level so the buildings along the canal don't lean. If the railing is crowded, try the alternatives: Punta della Dogana, for the church next to the customs house with open water behind, or Calle del Traghetto Vecchio, for a front-on view with gondolas in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky near the dome to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the white stone is not washed out. At blue hour, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep the phone steady. Wait for the countdown to finish before you move.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset and blue hour are the favourites, but the bridge gets very busy and you may have to jostle for railing space. For fewer people, a local photographer's guide suggests about 6:45 to 7:30 AM in December and January. Check sunrise and sunset times for your actual date.

text.access_note: The Ponte dell'Accademia and the canal-side views are open public space, but the Salute is a working church, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and dress.
claims_not_in_sources: Churches in Venice usually expect covered shoulders and knees, so a dress code may apply at the Salute.
Tapping the sky and lowering the exposure slider will keep the sky colour and stop the white stone being overexposed.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) makes distant subjects look smaller in the frame.
Resting elbows on a railing helps keep a phone steady during a night mode shot.

name: St Mark's Clock Tower
label: St Mark's Clock Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza San Marco' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza San Marco' (way/172349507): middle (279 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/410344943: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St Mark's Clocktower' (30 m across).
notes: Renaissance clock tower at the entrance to the Merceria.

text.description:
The Clock Tower stands on the north side of Piazza San Marco, where the Merceria, the main street towards the Rialto, leaves the square through its two-storey archway. It is an early Renaissance building. The tower and clock date from the 1490s, with building under way in 1496 and 1497 and the opening on 1 February 1499. The face is blue and gold, with a marble ring of the 24 hours, the zodiac, the sun pointer, and a little earth and moon at the centre. Higher up are a gilded Virgin and Child, the winged Lion of St Mark against a starry blue background, and, on the roof terrace, the two bronze figures known as the Moors, who strike the hours on a bell cast in 1497.

It photographs well because every layer is a different colour and texture, and the open square gives you room to step back and fit the whole tower in. On a phone, start wide, then zoom in for the clock face and the Moors. Keep the vertical lines straight by holding the phone level, and turn on gridlines to help. Tap the clock face to set focus and pull the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright. There may be scaffolding in the square, so check how it looks on the day.
text.geographic_location: On the north side of Piazza San Marco, at the entrance to the Merceria, joined to the eastern end of the Procuratie Vecchie.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stop serves this spot, so head for Piazza San Marco itself. The Merceria runs from the Rialto to the Piazza, and the tower's archway is where it enters the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole tower in the square. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if scaffolding, crowds or a close position stop you getting it all in. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clock face, the Lion and the Moors.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza San Marco (far end of the square, near the Basilica, looking northeast toward the tower). The whole tower with its clock face and the Moors above it, framed by the open square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it stands straight. Leave some of the square in the foreground, then take a second, zoomed-in shot of the clock and the Moors. For a different view, the Piazzetta San Marco end of the square shows the tower with the Basilica and Doge's Palace nearby. In the Mercerie you can frame the clock dial on the street side through the archway.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the clock face to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the blue and gold stay rich and the sky is not washed out. In low evening light, night mode can help, but hold the phone very still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late evening, for softer light and fewer crowds.

text.access_note: The tower's outside is easy to photograph from the open square, but going inside or up to the terrace is only possible on advance-booked guided tours, so check the official site before you go.

name: Ca' d'Oro
label: Ca' d'Oro
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Riva de l'Ogio' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Riva de l'Ogio nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/162227289: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ca' d'Oro' (56 m across).
notes: Ornate Gothic palace on the Grand Canal.

text.description:
Ca' d'Oro, the "House of Gold", is a Gothic palace on the Grand Canal. It was built between 1421 and 1437 for Marino Contarini, and it takes its name from the gilding and colour that once decorated its walls. Today it is a museum, the Galleria Giorgio Franchetti alla Ca' d'Oro, open since 1927. It is often described as the best-surviving palazzo in Venetian Gothic style.

It photographs well because the whole front is a pattern. Lacy arched loggias and quatrefoil openings (four-lobed, like a clover) rise in three storeys, and the facade is deliberately asymmetrical. Seen from the water's edge, the palace fills the frame, with boats passing in front of it.

For the full facade, go to Riva de l'Ogio. The best spot is at the far end of Riva de l'Ogio near Calle del Campaniel, on a wooden pontoon that reaches onto the Grand Canal. From there the palace is in view straight on, from across the water. Guides single this out as the land-based spot that frames the entire front. If the vaporetto stop beside the palace gets in the way, try the Rialto Mercato side, which gives a more distant, quieter angle on the same facade.

Photography inside the gallery has conflicting rules, so check the signs on arrival. The loggia is part of the ticketed museum.
text.geographic_location: Ca' d'Oro stands on the left bank of the Grand Canal, not far from the Rialto Bridge and the Rialto market. Its neighbour is the Palazzo Giustinian Pesaro.
text.directions_text: No Underground-style or tram stops apply in Venice, so the simplest way is on foot. Start at the Rialto market and follow the waterfront along the Grand Canal until you reach Riva de l'Ogio, then walk to its far end near Calle del Campaniel, where the wooden pontoon is. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which takes in the whole palace from across the water. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the loggia arches and the roofline pinnacles. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want more water and sky, because it makes the palace look smaller and bends the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Riva de l'Ogio (at its far end near Calle del Campaniel, on the wooden pontoon that extends onto the Grand Canal). The full Gothic facade of Ca' d'Oro seen straight on from across the water, with the whole palazzo in frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line up the roofline with a horizontal line so the facade does not lean. Keep the palace central, and leave a strip of water at the bottom for boat reflections. If a vaporetto or its stop blocks the view, wait for a gap or try the quieter Rialto Mercato angle on the other side of the canal. With the telephoto, frame just the three tiers of tracery for a detail shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale stone does not turn white. Try a Live Photo, so you can pick a frame with a boat in a good place.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides suggest late afternoon light for the facade, but this is not tied to this exact spot. Look at the light on the day and move if the front is in deep shade.

text.access_note: Riva de l'Ogio is public waterfront space, but the palace interior and loggia belong to the ticketed gallery, so check the official site before you go and follow the photography signs on arrival.

name: Fondaco dei Tedeschi
label: Fondaco dei Tedeschi
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/138803475: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fontego dei Tedeschi' (82 m across).
notes: Historic trading house with a rooftop terrace near Rialto.

text.description:
The Fondaco dei Tedeschi stands on the Grand Canal right beside the Rialto Bridge. For centuries it was the hostel and warehouse of Venice's German merchants. The first building dates from 1228. After a fire in 1505 it was rebuilt between 1505 and 1508 in Renaissance style, around one large central courtyard on four floors. Today it is a department store, and the map's stand-here point puts you at the heart of the building.

It photographs well because of its scale and its details. The building is about 82 m across, so the simple, regular geometry of the courtyard suits a phone camera, with strong lines and layers of arches. The Islamic-influenced arches are worth noticing: large ones below and smaller ones above. On the outside, look up for the large wall clock installed in 1571 and the roofline merlons with circular cut-outs topped with spheres. The façades were once frescoed, said to be by Giorgione or Titian in 1508, but only faint fragments survive, so don't expect colour on the walls.

For your pictures, take one wide shot to show the whole space, then move in on a few details: an arch, a stair, the clock or the roofline. Keep your phone level with the gridlines so the vertical lines stay straight. Because this is a shop, some areas may have access limits, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: On the Grand Canal next to the Rialto Bridge, in Venice.
text.directions_text: Head to the Rialto Bridge, which the building stands right beside on the Grand Canal. The phone icon on the map is at the building itself, so once you reach the Rialto Bridge you are only a short walk from it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the courtyard and its tiers of arches, then use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clock, the roofline merlons and other details high up.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The map places the point at the centre of the building, which is around its large inner courtyard, so you are looking up and around at the surrounding floors rather than at one flat façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the arches and the building's vertical edges so everything looks straight. Include two or three levels of arches to show the layers, then take a tighter shot of one repeated detail. Outside, tilt up and use zoom to isolate the clock and the sphere-topped merlons against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the brightest part of the architecture, then lower the exposure slider slightly so bright areas do not wash out. Hold the phone steady with both hands, as indoor light can be dim.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even daylight, for example on a bright overcast day or outside the middle of the day, suits the stonework and avoids harsh shadows. If you want the courtyard quieter, try going early, but check the official site for when it is open.

text.access_note: The building now houses a department store, so access to the interior may be restricted; check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Even, soft daylight (such as overcast conditions) tends to suit photographing stonework and courtyards.
Interior spaces of a shop may be dim and may be quieter early in the day.

name: Ca' Pesaro
label: Ca' Pesaro
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ponte del Forner' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ponte del Forner' (way/1136159920): middle (6 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2382783: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ca' Pesaro' (90 m across).
notes: Baroque palace on the Grand Canal.

text.description: Ca' Pesaro is a large Baroque palace of pale marble that now holds Venice's modern art museum. Its Grand Canal front has two storeys of columns and arched windows above a heavily textured stone base. The rhythm of light and shadow across those arches is what makes it so photogenic. The architect Baldassarre Longhena began work in 1659, and he also designed the church of the Salute and Ca' Rezzonico. He died before it was finished, and Gian Antonio Gaspari completed the palace in 1710. In 1898 Duchess Felicita Bevilacqua La Masa left it to the city, and it became a museum of modern art. Inside are 19th and 20th century paintings and sculpture, including Klimt's Judith II. This spot is a quieter way to photograph the palace than the busy Grand Canal front. Stand on Ponte del Forner, the bridge over Rio de la Pergola, and look along the narrow canal. The palace's Baroque bulk fills the end of the water, with the Grand Canal just beyond. The canal walls and the bridge give you a natural frame and some depth. Ponte di Ca' Pesaro, a small stone footbridge also on Rio de la Pergola, is another option if you want the palace's side and facade close behind the footbridge. Hold your phone steady, and if people are crossing, wait for a gap before you take the shot.
text.geographic_location: Ca' Pesaro stands on the Grand Canal in Venice.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, tram or vaporetto stop right at this spot, so start from the Grand Canal frontage of Ca' Pesaro and walk south-west along the side canal to Ponte del Forner. It is about 250 m on foot. Looking back from the bridge, the palace lies to the north-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the canal, the water and the palace at the far end. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the bridge edge and canal walls as a strong frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the palace closer and flatten the view down the canal.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ponte del Forner (stand on the bridge over Rio de la Pergola, looking toward the Grand Canal). A canal view down Rio de la Pergola toward the Grand Canal, with Ca' Pesaro's Baroque bulk at the end of the water. If you want a different angle, Ponte di Ca' Pesaro, also on Rio de la Pergola, is a small stone footbridge with the palace's side and facade close behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the canal centred, with the palace on a vertical line. Let the water lead the eye towards it, and keep the horizon level. Include a little of the canal walls on both sides for a frame. For a second shot, try Ponte di Ca' Pesaro and use the small stone footbridge as a foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale marble keeps its detail. If anything moves through the frame, try a Live Photo and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light, in the morning or late in the afternoon, usually flatters pale stone. If people are crossing the bridge, wait for a gap so you can take your time.

text.access_note: The canal-side view from the bridge is public, but entry to the museum may be ticketed and photography inside is restricted by room and exhibition, so check the official site and the signs before you go.

name: Santa Maria dei Miracoli
label: Santa Maria Miracoli
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ponte dei Miracoli' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ponte dei Miracoli' (way/150843065): middle (6 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/138800840: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chiesa di Santa Maria dei Miracoli' (44 m across).

text.description: Santa Maria dei Miracoli is a small church in Cannaregio, often called the "marble church" because its walls are clad in pale and coloured marble. It was designed in 1481 by Pietro Lombardo with his sons Tullio and Antonio, and finished in 1489. It was built to house a painting of the Madonna that local people regarded as miraculous. The facade is the draw for a phone camera. It has rows of blind arches, circular windows, a semicircular pediment and inlaid squares, crosses, stars and wheels in different marbles. It sits on a small island, with a canal on one side and little squares at either end, so you can get the whole front in one frame with water in the foreground. The church was restored between 1990 and 1997, and the marble is clean and bright. The best photo is from the small bridge across the rio, where the canal frames the facade. If you want something wider, Ponte Santa Maria Nova gives a canal view that takes in the small square and the church's surroundings. The streets here are narrow, so you will often be shooting upwards in tight space. Wait a moment for passers-by to clear the bridge steps, and keep your phone level so the vertical lines stay straight.
text.geographic_location: In the sestiere of Cannaregio, on a small island north of Piazza San Marco and west of Santi Giovanni e Paolo, with the canal on one side and Campo Santa Maria Nova a short way off across a bridge.
text.directions_text: Make your way north of Piazza San Marco towards Campo Santa Maria Nova; the church stands just beside that square, across a bridge. Venice is walked rather than driven, so follow the signs and your map on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole facade with the canal in front. If the space is too tight to fit it all in, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use 2x or the telephoto to pick out details such as the pediment, the round windows and the marble patterns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ponte dei Miracoli (small bridge directly across the rio from the church). The church's marble facade framed by the canal in the foreground, the classic postcard composition.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the church's vertical edges. Keep some canal water at the bottom of the frame for a sense of depth. For a different view, try Ponte Santa Maria Nova, which shows the small square and the church's surroundings rather than the facade alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white marble does not wash out. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) sparingly, because it stretches the edges of the frame and can make the building lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the morning if you can, when there are usually fewer people on the bridge and in the lanes. Any soft, even daylight shows the marble colours well.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from public bridges and lanes, but the church is a place of worship and photography inside is restricted, so check the official site and any signs on site before you go in.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is usually quieter on the bridge and in the surrounding lanes.
Soft, even daylight shows the marble colours well.
Streets in this part of Venice are for walking; people usually go on foot.
Using the ultra-wide lens close to a building can stretch the edges and make it appear to lean.
